what_it_does: This work tackles a longstanding problem in portable medical devices like EEG and ECG monitors that use only two electrodes: massive electrical interference from the power supply (up to 133 volts peak-to-peak) couples into the patient's body and ground, drowning out the tiny brain/heart signals the device is trying to measure. The researchers designed a specialized amplifier chip that stays powered-efficient (4.6 microwatts, about the power of a hearing-aid battery) while filtering out this interference 102 million times better than traditional designs. The key innovation recognizes that interference couples differently through the patient's body capacitance versus the ground path, allowing separate treatment of each—not the assumption that they're symmetric that prior work relied on.
